hints: The test covers 6 months and the mean is 1.1 per month. Scale the Poisson mean to 6 months so $X \sim \text{Po}(\lambda)$ where $\lambda = 1.1 \times 6$.
The principal wants to know if injuries have **reduced**, so the critical region is in the lower tail. Start with $\text{P}(X \leqslant 1) = \text{e}^{-\lambda}(1 + \lambda)$ using your $\lambda$.
Next try the next value up: $\text{P}(X \leqslant 2) = \text{e}^{-\lambda}\left(1 + \lambda + \dfrac{\lambda^2}{2}\right)$.
Calculate both probabilities with your calculator's Poisson cdf (or by hand) and write them to 3 significant figures.
Compare each with the significance level 2% (0.02). The critical region is the largest set of the form $X \leqslant c$ whose probability does not go over 0.02.
The probability of a Type I error is the probability of landing in the critical region when $\text{H}_0$ is true: take the cumulative probability for your critical region from the earlier step.
walkthrough:
**Set up the distribution (this earns the B1)**

Let $X$ be the number of sports injuries in 6 months. Injuries happen at random at a steady rate, so a Poisson distribution is used. The rate is 1.1 per month, and we are watching for 6 months. Rates scale with time, so the mean for 6 months is

$$\lambda = 1.1 \times 6 = 6.6$$

Under the null hypothesis (no change in the mean), $X \sim \text{Po}(6.6)$.

**Decide which tail**

The principal wants to test whether the mean has been **reduced**. Evidence for a reduction would be an unusually **small** number of injuries, so the critical region is $X \leqslant c$ for some value $c$ (the lower tail). This is a one-tailed test at the 2% level, so we look for the largest $c$ with $\text{P}(X \leqslant c) \leqslant 0.02$.

**Try $c = 1$ (this earns the first M1)**

$\text{P}(X \leqslant 1)$ means $\text{P}(X = 0) + \text{P}(X = 1)$, using $\text{P}(X=r) = \text{e}^{-6.6}\dfrac{6.6^r}{r!}$:

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 1) = \text{e}^{-6.6}(1 + 6.6)$$

On your calculator, $\text{e}^{-6.6} = 0.0013604\ldots$ and $1 + 6.6 = 7.6$:

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 1) = 0.0013604 \times 7.6 = 0.010339\ldots = 0.0103 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$

**Try $c = 2$ (this earns the second M1 and, with both values, the A1)**

Add the $r = 2$ term. First $6.6^2 = 43.56$, then divide by $2! = 2$ to get $21.78$:

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 2) = \text{e}^{-6.6}\left(1 + 6.6 + \dfrac{6.6^2}{2}\right) = \text{e}^{-6.6}(1 + 6.6 + 21.78)$$

$$1 + 6.6 + 21.78 = 29.38$$

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 2) = 0.0013604 \times 29.38 = 0.03997\ldots = 0.0400 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$

Quick check: adding another term can only make the cumulative probability bigger, and indeed $0.0400 > 0.0103$.

**Choose the critical region (this earns the DA1)**

Compare each with the 2% significance level (0.02):

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 1) = 0.0103 < 0.02 \quad \checkmark$$

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 2) = 0.0400 > 0.02 \quad \times$$

$X \leqslant 1$ is inside the 2% level but adding 2 would take us over it. So the critical region is $X \leqslant 1$.

**Probability of a Type I error (this earns the B1 FT)**

A Type I error happens when $\text{H}_0$ is true but we land in the critical region and reject it anyway. Its probability is the probability of the critical region under $\text{H}_0$:

$$\text{P}(\text{Type I error}) = \text{P}(X \leqslant 1) = 0.0103$$

Note that it is **not** 0.02. The significance level is the most we allow; the actual probability is what the Poisson distribution gives, which is lower because the values are discrete.

hints: A Type I error means rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_0$ is actually true. Say what $\text{H}_0$ claims here, and what the principal would wrongly conclude, in terms of sports injuries.
walkthrough:
**What a Type I error is**

In any hypothesis test there are two ways of being wrong. A **Type I error** is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true. So we need to say it in words about injuries, not just give a definition.

Here $\text{H}_0$ says the mean number of injuries has not changed (it is still 1.1 a month). $\text{H}_1$ says it has decreased.

**Final answer**

A Type I error would be wrongly concluding that the mean number of sports injuries has decreased, when in fact it has not changed.

hints: Write the hypotheses about the Poisson mean for 6 months, $\lambda$, using the value you found in part (i). The principal expects a reduction, so $\text{H}_1$ is one-tailed.
Compare the observed total of 2 injuries with the critical region you found in part (i), or compare $\text{P}(X \leqslant 2)$ with 2%. Decide whether 2 is inside.
If 2 is outside the critical region you do not reject $\text{H}_0$; if inside you do. Then write the conclusion about the mean number of injuries, using the word "evidence" and not definite wording.
walkthrough:
**Write the hypotheses (this earns the B1)**

The parameter is $\lambda$, the mean number of injuries per 6 months. The null hypothesis is that nothing has changed and the alternative is that injuries have been reduced:

$$\text{H}_0: \lambda = 6.6 \qquad \text{H}_1: \lambda < 6.6$$

The 6.6 comes from $1.1 \times 6$ months, as in part (i). Under $\text{H}_0$, $X \sim \text{Po}(6.6)$.

**Compare the observed value with the critical region (this earns the M1)**

The observed number of injuries is $X = 2$. From part (i) the critical region is $X \leqslant 1$. Is 2 in it? No: $2 > 1$.

Equivalent check using probabilities: $\text{P}(X \leqslant 2) = 0.0400$, and $0.0400 > 0.02$. The probability of getting 2 or fewer injuries is bigger than the 2% significance level, so the result is not unusual enough.

The M1 is for saying that 2 is not in the critical region.

**Conclusion in context (this earns the A1 FT)**

Since 2 is not in the critical region, we do **not reject** $\text{H}_0$. In words: at the 2% level there is no evidence that the mean number of sports injuries per month has decreased. Avoid saying it has "definitely not changed" — we only say we lack evidence.

**Final answer**

2 is not in the critical region $X \leqslant 1$ (equivalently $\text{P}(X \leqslant 2) = 0.0400 > 0.02$), so do not reject $\text{H}_0$: there is no evidence, at the 2% level, that the mean number of sports injuries has decreased.

hints: Over 36 months the Poisson mean is $1.1 \times 36$, which is large (above 15). A large-mean Poisson is approximately normal with mean and variance both equal to that value.

"Fewer than 30" means $X \leqslant 29$. Moving from a discrete to a continuous distribution needs a continuity correction: use the boundary half a unit above 29, the largest value included. Standardise $z = \dfrac{\text{boundary} - \text{mean}}{\sqrt{\text{variance}}}$.
You want the lower tail. If your $z$ is negative, use symmetry: $\Phi(-a) = 1 - \Phi(a)$ where $a$ is the positive version of $z$.
Look up $\Phi(a)$, subtract from 1 and round to 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
**Why use a normal approximation (this earns the B1)**

Let $Y$ be the number of injuries in 36 months. Rates scale with time, so the Poisson mean is

$$1.1 \times 36 = 39.6$$

$Y \sim \text{Po}(39.6)$. Working out $\text{P}(Y \leqslant 29)$ exactly means adding 30 Poisson terms. But when the Poisson mean is large (a rule of thumb is more than 15), the distribution is close to symmetric and bell-shaped, so we approximate it with a normal distribution having the **same mean and the same variance** (for a Poisson, mean = variance):

$$Y \approx \text{N}(39.6,\ 39.6)$$

**Continuity correction (this is part of the first M1)**

$Y$ takes whole numbers only, while a normal variable is continuous. "Fewer than 30" means $Y = 29$ or lower, i.e. $Y \leqslant 29$. In the continuous version, the whole number 29 occupies the interval from 28.5 to 29.5, so "29 or fewer" ends at **29.5**:

$$\text{P}(Y < 30) = \text{P}(Y \leqslant 29) \approx \text{P}(Y_{\text{normal}} < 29.5)$$

**Standardise (this earns the first M1)**

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance: $\sqrt{39.6} = 6.2928\ldots$

$$z = \dfrac{29.5 - 39.6}{\sqrt{39.6}} = \dfrac{-10.1}{6.2928} = -1.6050\ldots = -1.605 \text{ (3 d.p.)}$$

The mark scheme allows this M1 even with a wrong or missing continuity correction, but you need it for the right answer.

**Use symmetry (this earns the second M1)**

We want the area to the left of $z = -1.605$. The tables only list positive $z$, so use symmetry:

$$\text{P}(Z < -1.605) = 1 - \Phi(1.605)$$

Sense check: 29.5 is well below the mean 39.6, so a small probability is expected.

**Look up (this earns the A1)**

From the normal table, $\Phi(1.605) \approx 0.9457$.

$$1 - 0.9457 = 0.0543$$

This is the mark scheme's value. A calculator that keeps $z$ unrounded can show $0.0542$ in the last digit; the difference only comes from rounding $z$ and from the table, and the scheme quotes $0.0543$.

**Final answer**

$$\text{P}(\text{fewer than 30 injuries in 36 months}) \approx 0.0543 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$
